jo-1956.blurb: In March 1956, King Hussein dismissed British commander Glubb Pasha and renamed the Arab Legion the Jordan Arab Army, completing Arabization of the military; the move strained British–Jordanian relations, contributed to the Suez Crisis, and shifted Jordan toward reliance on American security backing.

kz-2006.blurb: In February 2006, prominent opposition leader Altynbek Sarsenbayev was found executed near Almaty alongside his bodyguard and driver; ten people were convicted by August, but questions of ultimate political responsibility were never resolved, and the killing deepened international concern about Kazakhstan's suppression of political opposition.

kg-2005.blurb: In March 2005, mass protests over disputed parliamentary elections forced President Askar Akayev to flee and formally resign after 15 years in power; Kurmanbek Bakiyev won a new presidential election in July, though the transition did not produce stable democratic consolidation.

ly-2017.blurb: In February 2017, Italy and Libya's UN-backed Government of National Accord signed a memorandum of understanding committing Italy to fund and train the Libyan Coast Guard; Mediterranean crossings fell sharply from mid-2017, but human rights organisations documented systematic abuse of migrants held in Libyan detention facilities.

lt-2009.blurb: On 31 December 2009, Lithuania shut down Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant's Unit 2 as required by its EU accession agreement, instantly transforming the country from a net electricity exporter into a net importer and sharply increasing its dependence on Russian energy infrastructure.

ml-2000.blurb: In 2000, Mali qualified for approximately $870 million in total debt service relief under the HIPC Initiative, backed by IMF/World Bank structural adjustment programs including cotton sector reforms and privatization of public utilities, substantially reducing the country's debt burden.
sources: IMF press release pr0052 (original HIPC completion + Enhanced HIPC decision point, 2000, $870M figure)
IMF press release pr0329 (Enhanced HIPC completion point, early March 2003, ~$675M figure)

mr-2003.blurb: President Taya survived the June 2003 coup attempt and won re-election in November 2003, though opposition alleged widespread fraud and former head of state Haidalla was arrested on coup-plotting charges. Coup leader Hanenna was captured in late 2004 and sentenced to life imprisonment, but the underlying instability culminated in a successful coup that ousted Taya in August 2005.

mu-1985.blurb: In December 1985, four sitting Mauritian MPs were arrested at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport carrying roughly 20 kg of heroin on diplomatic passports — the "Amsterdam Affair" — halving the ruling coalition's parliamentary majority and prompting institutional anti-corruption and drug-enforcement reforms, though Prime Minister Jugnauth survived to win the 1987 elections.

mx-1985.blurb: The earthquake's aftermath galvanized Mexican civil society: citizens formed independent rescue brigades and grassroots organizations that mounted the first mass challenge to PRI's centralized authority in decades, accelerating a democratization process that ultimately ended the party's 71-year one-party rule.

md-2021.blurb: In July 2021, President Maia Sandu's Party of Action and Solidarity won a landslide snap parliamentary election, securing the first single-party absolute majority since 2001 and forming a government under Prime Minister Natalia Gavrilita — decisively shifting Moldova toward EU integration and away from Russian influence.

ma-2000.blurb: Following his 1999 accession, King Mohammed VI launched a transitional-justice opening, establishing a reparations commission for victims of the Hassan II-era "Years of Lead" that paved the way for the Equity and Reconciliation Commission (IER) in 2004 — the first truth commission worldwide empowered to directly award reparations.

mm-2001.blurb: By 2001, the Tatmadaw's campaign in Shan State had driven mass displacement of Shan civilians into Thailand and drew sustained international condemnation, while ethnic armed groups moved to coordinate political resistance against the military junta.

nz-2011.blurb: In 2011, Telecom New Zealand split into two publicly-listed companies — Chorus (wholesale infrastructure) and Telecom New Zealand (retail and mobile) — as a condition of participating in the government's Ultra-Fast Broadband initiative, permanently restructuring the country's telecommunications landscape.
sources: Fact-checker A feedback (name error + date inaccuracy)
Research facts (confirmed core: UFB initiative, Telecom NZ mandatory separation, two publicly-listed companies, Chorus wholesale / retail arm, permanent restructuring)

ni-2006.blurb: In November 2006, Nicaragua enacted a total abortion ban under outgoing President Bolaños, criminalizing the procedure under all circumstances; that same month, Daniel Ortega won the presidential election, returning the FSLN to power after 17 years and beginning a long trajectory of democratic backsliding.

mk-2015.blurb: The wiretapping scandal triggered mass protests and EU-brokered negotiations, forcing Prime Minister Gruevski to resign in January 2016; early elections followed, bringing opposition leader Zaev to power in 2017, while a Special Prosecutor charged over 90 individuals linked to the surveillance operation.

pk-2016.blurb: Following a militant attack on an Indian Army camp at Uri in September 2016 that killed 19 soldiers, India conducted surgical strikes across the Line of Control targeting militant camps in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, triggering a sharp diplomatic rupture and a prolonged period of heightened border skirmishing between the two nuclear-armed states through 2018.

ps-2000.blurb: The Second Intifada erupted in September 2000 following the collapse of Camp David peace talks and Ariel Sharon's visit to the al-Aqsa compound, triggering a sustained armed uprising that lasted until 2005, collapsed the Oslo peace process, and set the stage for Hamas's 2006 electoral victory.

pa-1981.blurb: Torrijos's death in a plane crash on July 31, 1981 shattered Panama's political coalition; a succession of short-lived military leaders followed until General Manuel Noriega consolidated control by 1983, establishing a dictatorship that lasted until the U.S. military invasion in December 1989.

py-1989.blurb: In February 1989, General Andrés Rodríguez overthrew Alfredo Stroessner in a military coup, ending a 34-year dictatorship; Rodríguez swiftly lifted political bans, held multi-party elections, and won the presidency in May 1989, initiating Paraguay's democratic transition.

pe-1968.blurb: General Juan Velasco Alvarado's military government nationalized foreign-owned oil fields and enacted sweeping land reform, but Velasco was himself ousted in a second coup in August 1975 by Prime Minister Francisco Morales Bermudez, who subsequently reversed many of the reforms.

ph-1959.blurb: The Garcia administration's "Filipino First" policy, entrenched in 1959, strained relations with the IMF and the United States and became associated with exchange-control corruption; Garcia lost the 1961 election to Diosdado Macapagal, who dismantled the controls on an anti-corruption, liberalization platform.

ph-2001.blurb: Mass civilian protests at EDSA Shrine forced President Joseph Estrada from office in January 2001 after the military withdrew support; Vice President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo was sworn in as president on January 20, marking a people-power democratic transition that the Supreme Court later upheld as a constructive resignation.

pt-1999.blurb: On 1 January 1999, Portugal joined the eurozone as one of eleven founding members, irrevocably fixing the escudo to the euro and permanently transferring monetary policy authority to the European Central Bank.

qa-2002.blurb: In December 2002, Qatar and the United States signed a Defense Cooperation Agreement formalizing the US military presence at Al Udeid Air Base; by April 2003, the US Combat Air Operations Center had relocated there from Saudi Arabia, making Al Udeid the largest American military installation in the Middle East.

ro-1990.blurb: Ion Iliescu and the ex-communist National Salvation Front won Romania's first free elections in May 1990, then weeks later summoned thousands of coal miners to violently crush anti-government protesters in Bucharest — an episode that severely damaged Romania's democratic credibility abroad and delayed its Euro-Atlantic integration.

ru-1989.blurb: The strikes politicized Soviet workers and catalysed independent labour organizing; a second strike wave in March 1991 saw miners openly demand Gorbachev's resignation. The movement is widely credited as a contributing factor to the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991.

so-1970.blurb: In 1970, Siad Barre's Supreme Revolutionary Council nationalized foreign banks and major industries as part of Somalia's declaration as a Socialist State, inaugurating a state-control program whose chronic inefficiencies weakened the economy and contributed to the collapse of the Barre regime and descent into civil war in 1991.

so-1995.blurb: Following the UN withdrawal in March 1995, warlord Mohamed Farrah Aidid declared himself interim president in June 1995, but the claim went unrecognized internationally; factional civil war continued until Aidid was fatally wounded in July 1996, leaving Somalia without a functioning central government.

lk-1972.blurb: In May 1972, Sri Lanka adopted its first republican constitution, sidelining Tamil minority participation, entrenching Sinhala as the sole official language, and removing judicial review of legislation — a rupture widely identified as the proximate political cause of the civil war that followed in 1983.

se-1992.blurb: Under intense speculative pressure, Sweden abandoned its ECU peg on 19 November 1992 and floated the krona, which depreciated sharply; the Riksbank subsequently adopted a 2% inflation target in January 1993, anchoring a fiscal and banking-sector reform program that drove an export-led recovery through the mid-1990s.

sy-2019.blurb: On March 23, 2019, the Syrian Democratic Forces declared final victory at Baghuz Fawqani, eliminating ISIS's last territorial holdout and ending its physical caliphate; the group then transitioned into a dispersed insurgency, and its founder Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi was killed in a U.S. raid in October 2019.

tz-1986.blurb: In 1986, Tanzania under President Mwinyi reversed a decade of resistance to IMF conditionality by adopting the Economic Recovery Programme, which introduced currency devaluation, price liberalization, and cuts to state controls — marking the effective end of Nyerere's Ujamaa socialist model and the beginning of sustained structural adjustment through the 1990s.

th-1971.blurb: Thanom's self-coup triggered deepening popular resistance, culminating in a mass uprising in October 1973 when over 250,000 demonstrators took to Bangkok's streets; after troops fired on the crowd, King Bhumibol intervened and Thanom, Praphat, and Narong fled into exile, ending the military regime.

tn-1974.blurb: Bourguiba reversed course within weeks, collapsing the proposed union almost immediately and straining Tunisia-Libya relations for years.
sources: Fact-checker feedback A and B (both place constitutional amendment in March 1975, not 1974)

tn-2021.blurb: On 25 July 2021, President Kais Saied suspended parliament and dismissed the prime minister in what observers widely termed a self-coup; he subsequently ruled by decree, dissolved parliament outright, and in July 2022 enacted a new constitution concentrating power in the presidency, effectively dismantling Tunisia's post-Arab Spring democratic order.

tr-1994.blurb: Turkey's 1994 currency crisis triggered a severe recession and the government responded with an IMF-backed stabilisation package in April 1994; recovery was short-lived, as incomplete structural reforms left the economy vulnerable to a deeper crisis in 2001.

tr-2016.blurb: Following the defeated coup, President Erdogan declared a two-year state of emergency and launched sweeping purges — detaining roughly 80,000 people and dismissing or suspending around 150,000 officials, military officers, judges, and journalists — while a 2017 referendum abolished Turkey's parliamentary system and consolidated presidential power.

tm-1999.blurb: In December 1999, Turkmenistan's parliament — seated in uncontested elections boycotted by the OSCE — abolished presidential term limits and formally declared Saparmurat Niyazov President for Life, concentrating unchecked executive power in him until his death in 2006.

ug-2020.blurb: Uganda recorded its first COVID-19 case in March 2020, prompting President Museveni to impose one of Africa's strictest lockdowns; the resulting economic contraction drove an estimated three million additional Ugandans into poverty and deepened political discontent ahead of the January 2021 election.

gb-1963.blurb: In January 1963, French President Charles de Gaulle vetoed the UK's application to join the European Economic Community, citing British ties to the United States and an incompatible economic structure. The UK was kept out of the EEC for a decade, finally acceding in 1973 under Prime Minister Edward Heath.

gb-1997.blurb: Days after Labour's 1997 landslide, Chancellor Gordon Brown granted the Bank of England independence to set interest rates, ending direct ministerial control over monetary policy — a reform formalised by the Bank of England Act 1998 and widely adopted as a global template for central bank independence.

us-1950.blurb: When North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950, the Truman administration used the crisis to enact NSC-68, rapidly expanding the US military and transforming the document into the blueprint for America's Cold War military posture through the end of the Soviet Union.

ve-2010.blurb: Venezuela severed diplomatic ties with Colombia in July 2010 after President Uribe accused Caracas of harboring FARC guerrillas, but the rupture was swiftly reversed when incoming Colombian President Santos met Chávez in Santa Marta on 10 August, restoring full bilateral relations through UNASUR-mediated dialogue.

ye-1957.blurb: Egypt dispatched a military mission to Yemen in 1957 at Imam Ahmad's request, accompanied by Soviet-bloc arms and advisers; the Egyptian officers' Nasserist influence helped inspire Yemeni Free Officers who overthrew the Imamate in the September 1962 revolution, triggering a prolonged Egyptian military intervention.

zm-1972.blurb: Zambia became a one-party state under UNIP in December 1972, consolidating power under President Kaunda for 18 years until growing popular discontent forced a return to multiparty elections in 1991, when Kaunda was voted out of office.

zm-1973.blurb: Zambia's 1973 constitution entrenched UNIP as the sole legal party, and Kaunda ruled under a one-party state for 18 years until economic collapse and social unrest forced a return to multiparty politics — which Kaunda lost to Frederick Chiluba in October 1991.

dz-1971.blurb: On February 24, 1971, President Boumediene decreed the nationalization of Algeria's hydrocarbon industry, transferring majority control of French oil operations and full control of natural gas infrastructure to state company Sonatrach, sharply rupturing Franco-Algerian relations and cementing sovereign control over the country's energy wealth.

dz-2020.blurb: In November 2020, President Tebboune's constitutional referendum passed with 66.8% approval but on a record-low turnout of 23.7%, as the Hirak movement — which had ousted Bouteflika in 2019 — boycotted the vote and rejected it as a democratic facade, deepening political illegitimacy rather than demobilising dissent.

am-1999.blurb: On 27 October 1999, five gunmen stormed the Armenian National Assembly and killed Prime Minister Vazgen Sargsyan, Parliament Speaker Karen Demirchyan, and six others; the attack eliminated the parliamentary leadership that had checked President Kocharyan's power and accelerated Armenia's drift toward semi-authoritarian presidential rule.

am-2016.blurb: The April 2016 Four-Day War — the worst fighting in Nagorno-Karabakh since the 1994 ceasefire — ended with a Russia-brokered ceasefire on 5 April, with Azerbaijan retaining small territorial gains; international mediation resumed but the conflict escalated into a decisive Azerbaijani victory in the 2020 Second Nagorno-Karabakh War.

au-2018.blurb: In January 2018, the Turnbull Government launched Australia's first Defence Export Strategy, fundamentally repositioning the country's defence industry from a self-defence orientation toward active global arms exporting, backed by a new Defence Export Office and a $3.8 billion export credit facility.

bh-1993.blurb: The advisory council failed to satisfy demands for genuine democratic participation, and political unrest erupted in December 1994 — sustained protests and clashes with security forces that continued until 1999, when Emir Hamad's accession opened the path to substantive constitutional reform.
sources: Research facts provided in prompt: Bahrain Consultative Council 1992/1993, December 1994 uprising, 1999 accession of Emir Hamad, National Action Charter 2001, constitutional monarchy 2002

bh-1995.blurb: The uprising intensified through 1999, ending only after Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa became Emir; a 2001 referendum on the National Action Charter passed by a large majority, ushering in a constitutional transition and the release of political prisoners including al-Jamri.

bd-2010.blurb: Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal, established under Sheikh Hasina's Awami League government to prosecute 1971 Liberation War atrocities, issued its first arrest warrants against senior Jamaat-e-Islami leaders in July 2010; it ultimately executed six individuals, triggered deep political polarisation, and drew sustained international criticism over fair-trial standards.

be-2019.blurb: Belgium's May 2019 federal elections produced a deeply fragmented result — with Vlaams Belang surging in Flanders — triggering a government formation crisis of nearly 500 days before the seven-party "Vivaldi coalition" under Alexander De Croo was sworn in on 1 October 2020.

bo-2008.blurb: The massacre galvanized regional condemnation and isolated the eastern opposition; within months, Morales negotiated a path to a new constitutional referendum (January 2009) that enshrined indigenous rights and resource nationalization, consolidating rather than ending his presidency.

br-1975.blurb: The deal triggered sharp US opposition and a geopolitical rupture — Brazil cancelled its military agreement with Washington in 1977. The technology transfer largely failed; of the eight planned reactors under the agreement, only one reached operation.
sources: RESEARCH FACTS provided in prompt — Brazil–West Germany Nuclear Agreement 1975 outcome section

br-2005.blurb: Brazil's Mensalão scandal erupted in June 2005 when it emerged that the ruling Workers' Party had paid legislators monthly stipends for their votes; senior PT officials resigned and President Lula survived impeachment threats, though he won re-election in 2006, and 25 defendants were ultimately convicted by the Supreme Court in 2012.

br-2012.blurb: In early 2012, Brazil briefly surpassed the United Kingdom to become the world's sixth-largest economy — the peak of its commodity-driven boom — before subsequent policy interventionism contributed to a sharp recession and Brazil fell back in the rankings.

bi-2015.blurb: Nkurunziza won the disputed election and remained in power, but Burundi descended into prolonged crisis: hundreds were killed, over 400,000 fled to neighbouring countries, and the EU and US imposed sanctions and froze aid — a situation that persisted until Nkurunziza's death in 2020.

cm-2020.blurb: The ruling CPDM swept Cameroon's February 2020 parliamentary and municipal elections, winning the vast majority of seats, even as Anglophone separatists boycotted, kidnapped candidates, and burned election offices — and subsequently assassinated several newly elected local officials — leaving the Anglophone armed conflict unresolved.
